results.summary: This project is described as a test to try fabricating a chip with some special function other than simple logic. The documentation is extremely thin and does not specify what the logic actually does or how it should behave. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs, but no external hardware is required according to the description. The design appears to be a learning exercise or template rather than a complete, documented circuit.

The project is titled '3 Bit Adder' and is intended to add two 3-bit numbers, producing a sum and carry. The documentation consists only of the placeholder word 'dup' for both the how-it-works and how-to-test sections, so no actual implementation details are provided. It uses six inputs and four outputs, which is consistent with a 3-bit adder with carry-in and carry-out. No external hardware is required, but the lack of documentation makes it impossible to verify the design's functionality.

This design implements an 8-to-3 encoder that, according to the description, displays the letter 'U' on a 7-segment display when a specific 8-port switch code is set. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs, with the outputs presumably driving the segments of the display. The documentation is minimal and does not explain the encoding scheme or the exact switch pattern required. External hardware includes an 8-port switch and a 7-segment display.

The project is titled 'Simple NAND 2' and is described as a work in progress with documentation that will follow later. The how-it-works and how-to-test sections contain placeholder text, so the actual functionality is unknown. It has eight inputs and three outputs, which might suggest a simple logic gate implementation, but this is not confirmed. The external hardware list includes an LED display, a flux compensator, and a quantum computer, which appears to be a joke and not a serious requirement.

This design sums eight input signals, treating them as the numbers 1 through 10, and displays the last digit of the sum on a 7-segment display. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs, with the outputs connected to the segments of the display. The project is intended as a simple test or educational example, and it requires an external 7-segment display to show the result. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation.

The project is titled 'nothing-yet' and has no actual design implemented. The documentation explicitly states that there is no design yet and that the how-to-test section is a placeholder. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, but no functionality is described. No external hardware is required, and the project appears to be an empty template.

This project is a counter that counts to 4, as indicated by its title and one-line description. It divides the frequency of an input clock to produce an output signal that drives an LED. The design has a single output pin labeled 'Signal_to_led' and no inputs, suggesting it uses an internal clock or the clock is provided elsewhere. The documentation is very sparse, and the external hardware section is left as a template placeholder.

This design displays a simple snake pattern on a 7-segment display, advancing with each clock cycle. It was created during a Wokwi workshop and requires an external 7-segment indicator, with the decimal point unused. The design lacks reset logic, so the initial state is unpredictable, and it has no debounce, meaning a physical button clock source will not work reliably. It uses one input for the clock and eight outputs for the display segments.

This sequential circuit spells out the phrase 'tinytapeoutrocks' symbol by symbol on a 7-segment display, advancing on each clock edge. It is designed to run at 2 Hz or in manual clock mode, where pressing a button cycles through the 16 symbols. The eight outputs must be connected to the display segments in the classic order, and no external hardware is needed beyond the display. The project is notable for its simple, self-contained operation and clear documentation.

This design acts as a secret code detector: it turns on an output when inputs 1, 2, 3, 4, and 8 are all active. It uses eight inputs and one output, which can drive an LED to indicate the correct combination. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand the basic function. External hardware needed includes an 8-input device (such as switches) and an output LED.
